claims.claim: Intrinsic motivation means acting because the activity is inherently interesting or satisfying, while extrinsic motivation means acting for a separable outcome; extrinsic motivation varies considerably in relative autonomy and can reflect either external control or genuine self-regulation.
Self-determination theory names autonomy, competence, and relatedness as basic psychological needs whose support underlies intrinsic motivation and the internalization of extrinsic reasons.

The named regulation types have different empirical profiles: across 344 samples and 223,209 participants, intrinsic motivation related to student success and well-being, identified regulation was particularly strongly related to persistence, introjected regulation related to persistence and performance goals but also to indicators of ill-being, and external regulation was not associated with performance or persistence but was associated with decreased well-being.

Expectancy-value theory as developed by Eccles, Wigfield and colleagues centres on ability beliefs, expectancies for success, and the components of subjective task value, and relates them to performance and to choice of activities.

In 2020 Eccles and Wigfield renamed the framework situated expectancy-value theory, explicitly to counter readings of the model as static, linear, and monolithic, to foreground the elaborated cost component of task value, and to stress the impact of situation and cultural background on the development of expectancies and values.

Attribution theory sorts causal explanations for outcomes along three dimensions - locus (internal or external), stability (permanent or changeable), and controllability - and internal, controllable attributions such as effort and strategy support continued motivation while stable, uncontrollable ones undermine it.

Attribution retraining works only when the redirected cause is genuine: the open educational psychology literature pairs it with appropriately difficult tasks, individual help, and specific feedback rather than generic exhortations to try harder.

Mastery goals define success as understanding or personal improvement and are associated with deeper, more durable learning, while performance goals define success relative to others; performance-avoidance goals aim only at not looking incompetent and are linked to self-handicapping.

Achievement goal findings depend on measurement: across 243 correlational studies with 91,087 participants, performance-approach scales composed mostly of normatively referenced items correlated positively with performance outcomes (r = .14) while scales dominated by appearance and evaluative items correlated negatively (r = -.14), leading the authors to conclude that researchers use the same label for conceptually different constructs.

A 1999 meta-analysis of 128 experiments found expected tangible rewards reduced free-choice intrinsic motivation (engagement-contingent d = -0.40, completion-contingent d = -0.36, performance-contingent d = -0.28) while positive feedback increased free-choice behaviour (d = 0.33) and self-reported interest (d = 0.31).

The undermining finding is contested: Eisenberger and Cameron argued in 1996 that detrimental effects of reward occur only under restricted, easily avoidable conditions, and a 2014 meta-analysis of 183 samples and 212,468 participants found intrinsic motivation predicted performance with or without incentives, mattered less when incentives were directly tied to performance, and that incentives better predicted quantity of performance while intrinsic motivation better predicted quality.

The National Study of Learning Mindsets, a preregistered randomized trial with 12,490 ninth graders in 65 nationally representative U.S. schools, found a short online growth mindset intervention raised lower-achieving students' core-course GPA by 0.10 grade points (95% CI 0.04-0.16) and raised advanced tenth-grade mathematics enrolment by about 3 percentage points, from 33% to 36%, with effects concentrated where peer norms aligned with the intervention message.

Meta-analytic evidence on growth mindset is weak: Sisk and colleagues (2018) reported weak overall effects across a correlational meta-analysis (k = 273, N = 365,915) and an intervention meta-analysis (k = 43, N = 57,155), with some support for benefits among low-socioeconomic-status or academically at-risk students, and Macnamara and Burgoyne (2023) found an overall intervention effect of d = 0.05 across 63 studies (N = 97,672) that was non-significant after correcting for publication bias and d = 0.02 among the highest-quality studies.

A 2007 IES practice guide recommended teaching students that academic abilities are expandable and improvable, and rated that recommendation as supported by moderate evidence; it also rated prescriptive, informational feedback as moderate.

A randomized field experiment in high school science classes found that writing about connections between course content and students' own lives increased interest in science and course grades specifically for students with low expectations of success.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
positions: Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999): expected tangible rewards reliably reduce free-choice intrinsic motivation, with tangible rewards more detrimental for children than college students; positive feedback enhances it.
Eisenberger and Cameron (1996): detrimental effects occur only under restricted, easily avoidable conditions, and conditioning mechanisms explain both increases and decreases.

Cerasoli, Nicklin and Ford (2014): intrinsic motivation and incentives jointly predict performance and are not necessarily antagonistic; crowding out appears when incentives are directly tied to performance.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the disagreement, gives the effect sizes from the 1999 meta-analysis, and adopts the 2014 synthesis as the practical reading: what the incentive is tied to matters, incentives predict quantity while intrinsic motivation predicts quality. The mechanism framing here (a directly contingent payment installs external rather than identified regulation) is deliberately different from the contingency-design framing in education:learning-theories:behaviorism so the two lessons do not duplicate each other.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether growth mindset interventions improve achievement
positions: Mindset theory as promoted by Dweck and colleagues: believing ability is malleable improves responses to difficulty and achievement, and short interventions can shift it.
Yeager et al. (2019, Nature): a nationally representative preregistered trial found real but small effects, limited to lower-achieving students and to schools whose peer norms supported the message.
Sisk et al. (2018) and Macnamara & Burgoyne (2023): overall effects are weak to null, with evidence of publication and researcher bias, and near-zero effects in the highest-quality subset.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents mindset as contested, quotes the NSLM effect sizes as small and conditional, reports the meta-analytic nulls including the bias findings, and explicitly declines to present mindset interventions as reliably transformative. The 2007 IES 'moderate evidence' rating is reported as a dated recommendation rather than as current support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether performance goals help or hurt achievement
positions: Textbook synthesis: mastery goals produce deeper learning; performance goals can raise grades but not depth; performance-avoidance goals are harmful.
Hulleman et al. (2010): goal-outcome correlations flip sign depending on scale wording, so the field is using one label for different constructs.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the textbook distinction as a first approximation and then reports the measurement finding with the two contrasting correlations, instructing students to ask what the items actually said.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive motivation content: it described 'Motivation And Learning' as a generic foundational concept, defined it circularly as 'a foundational Education concept covered in this lesson', and offered a toolbox-drawer analogy and three content-free quiz items. None of it was retained.
The draft's title casing 'Motivation And Learning' was incorrect.
The draft carried no sources at all and an eight-minute estimate that does not match the material.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with sourced content covering self-determination theory, situated expectancy-value theory, attribution theory, and achievement goal theory.
Corrected the title to 'Motivation and Learning'.
Added the two contested areas the popular literature oversimplifies (reward undermining and growth mindset) with effect sizes and null results rather than slogans.
Kept self-efficacy deliberately brief and cross-referenced to education:learning-theories:social-learning-theory.
Reused the exact source ids and URLs already registered by education:learning-theories:behaviorism for the three shared reward-debate sources so the registry stays consistent.
rightsIssues: Most scholarly sources are paywalled journal articles used as REFERENCE_ONLY; abstracts and metadata were verified through the Europe PMC and Crossref APIs and all prose in the lesson is original synthesis.
Seifert & Sutton's Educational Psychology is CC BY 3.0 as displayed on LibreTexts; it is credited, and no wording was reproduced from it.
The IES practice guide is a U.S. federal government publication; its recommendation wording is quoted only in short form and attributed.

Elliot & McGregor (2001) and Weiner (1985) were verified at metadata level only (Crossref and Europe PMC records; abstracts are not distributed openly). Substantive claims attributed to them are independently supported by the CC BY textbook and by Hulleman et al. (2010), and this is recorded in their source notes.

sourceRecords.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivations: Classic Definitions and New Directions
sourceRecords.provider: Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L., Contemporary Educational Psychology 25(1), 2000
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API (PMID 10620381, doi 10.1006/ceps.1999.1020). Supports the classic intrinsic/extrinsic definitions, the argument that extrinsic motivation varies in relative autonomy and can reflect external control or true self-regulation, and the relation of both classes of motive to the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness.

sourceRecords.title: From expectancy-value theory to situated expectancy-value theory: A developmental, social cognitive, and sociocultural perspective on motivation
